# Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization


## Overview
Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization is a family of approaches designed to mitigate the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when supervision from multiple viewpoints is sparse [S1, unofficial][S2]. By applying geometric or semantic priors, these methods prevent overfitting to observed views and improve generalization to unseen ones [S1, unofficial]. This family addresses artifacts like "floaters" and "background collapse" common in sparse-input settings [S2]. Unlike progressive reconstruction methods that restrain model capacity over time, this family relies on explicit regularization terms to guide the optimization toward geometrically plausible solutions [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves augmenting the standard photometric loss with auxiliary constraints that enforce consistency across views or adherence to prior knowledge about scene geometry [S1, unofficial]. Geometric priors stabilize the learned density field or Gaussian distribution by applying smoothness or normal consistency constraints [S1, unofficial]. Semantic regularization enforces cross-view consistency by leveraging high-level scene structure to align reconstructions with expected object layouts [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Unseen Viewpoint Regularization
Unseen Viewpoint Regularization is a module designed to mitigate background collapse and overfitting in sparse-input settings by regularizing 3DGS training at viewpoints different from the input views [S2]. It is chosen when training data is extremely sparse and standard photometric loss leads to artifacts like floaters or empty backgrounds [S2]. The method splits regularization based on the distance of the novel view from training cameras [S2]. For viewpoints distant from training cameras, it incorporates a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to provide geometric priors [S2]. For viewpoints close to training cameras, it incorporates a depth warping loss, which uses traditional transformations to re-render depth and color from novel view points and enforces consistency [S2].

## Background
The challenge of reconstructing scenes from sparse views is critical in real-world settings where dense multi-view captures are impractical [S1, unofficial]. Early solutions focused on constraining variation between views, such as DietNeRF, which added constraints to ensure high-level semantic features remained the same across views [S2]. More recently, with the advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting, methods like SparseGS have introduced specific modules like Unseen Viewpoint Regularization to address the unique artifacts of Gaussian representations, such as floaters, by combining SDS losses with depth-based constraints [S2]. The broader family of regularization approaches contrasts with progressive reconstruction techniques like FreeNeRF and Nerfies, which restrain model complexity over time rather than adding explicit loss terms [S1, unofficial].
